content:
I realized something cool today (although it's likely to be well-known among experienced users, that is, most people who will read this.)

Suppose I want to prove the following theorem.

import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Fin

variable {R : Type*} [DecidableEq R]

example (a b c d e f : R) : ({a, b, c} : Finset R).product {d, e, f} =
      {(a, d), (a, e), (a, f), (b, d), (b, e), (b, f), (c, d), (c, e), (c, f)} := by
  ext ⟨x, y⟩
  simp
  tauto

While this works, it's rather inelegant that tauto is needed (since tauto is likely to take exponential time in the number of variables). Logically, this theorem should be easy to construct: you want to “explicitly calculate” the product of two finite sets, and the resulting set is easily calculated programmatically from both sets: for each element in the first set, pair it with every element in the second set.

With simp, one can write a rudimentary “calculation engine”, although this method is restricted to relatively simple pattern matching. If I have the following lemmas:

theorem Finset.product_insert_left (a : R) (u v : Finset R) :
    (insert a u).product v = v.image (a, ·) ∪ u.product v := by
  simp only [Finset.product_eq_sprod, Finset.insert_eq, Finset.union_product,
    Finset.singleton_product, Finset.map_eq_image]
  rfl

theorem Finset.product_singleton_left (a : R) (v : Finset R) :
    ({a} : Finset R).product v = v.image (a, ·) := by
  ext ⟨x, y⟩
  simp [Finset.product_eq_sprod, Finset.mem_image, eq_comm]

then I can write the proof above with just one simp:

example (a b c d e f : R) :
    ({a, b, c} : Finset R).product ({d, e, f} : Finset R) =
      {(a, d), (a, e), (a, f), (b, d), (b, e), (b, f), (c, d), (c, e), (c, f)} := by
  simp only [Finset.product_insert_left, Finset.product_singleton_left,
    Finset.image_insert, Finset.image_singleton, Finset.singleton_union, Finset.insert_union]

Furthermore, this is faster (I think it's around O(n²), much better than exponential).

That said, the method above is rather limited: suppose I want to prove a theorem of the form

example (a b c d : R) : ({a, b, c, d} : Finset R) = {c, b, a, a, d} := by sorry

I suppose I would need to write a tactic.

But writing a tactic seems to be harder in general. (I was reading through the compute_degree tactic and it looks really scary, even though it doesn't _sound_ that difficult on paper. I suppose one reason is that it tries to be very general? Still, if one isn't that ambitious, it shouldn't be that difficult?)

aesop closes this goal in a reasonable time

example (a b c d e f : R) : ({a, b, c} : Finset R).product {d, e, f} =
      {(a, d), (a, e), (a, f), (b, d), (b, e), (b, f), (c, d), (c, e), (c, f)} := by
  ext; aesop

For these kinds of explicit calculations, writing a simproc to do this for you would definitely be an option. (Though the fact that aesop can do it already weakens a case for prioritising writing this simproc.)

Good to know about simproc.

It isn't too difficult to come up with one that doesn't work with aesop.

import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
import Mathlib.Data.Fin.VecNotation

variable {R : Type*} [DecidableEq R]

/-- Convert a function from a finite type to any type to the element type of `Finset.univ.pi`. -/
abbrev toUnivPi {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (v : ι → R) :
    (i : ι) → i ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset ι) → R := λ i _ ↦ v i

example (a b : R) :
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 3)).pi (λ _ ↦ ({a, b} : Finset R)) =
      {toUnivPi ![a, a, a], toUnivPi ![a, a, b], toUnivPi ![a, b, a], toUnivPi ![a, b, b],
       toUnivPi ![b, a, a], toUnivPi ![b, a, b], toUnivPi ![b, b, a], toUnivPi ![b, b, b]} := by
  sorry

example (a b c : R) :
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 3)).pi ![{a, b}, {b, c}, {c}] =
      {toUnivPi ![a, b, c], toUnivPi ![a, c, c], toUnivPi ![b, b, c], toUnivPi ![b, c, c]} := by
  sorry

My (annoying) solution using simp:

import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Pi
import Mathlib.Data.Fin.VecNotation

variable {R : Type*} [DecidableEq R]

/-- Convert a function from a finite type to any type to the element type of `Finset.univ.pi`. -/
abbrev toUnivPi {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (v : ι → R) :
    (i : ι) → i ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset ι) → R := λ i _ ↦ v i

theorem univ_pi_eq_image_piFinset {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] (t : ι → Finset R) :
    Finset.univ.pi t = (Fintype.piFinset t).image toUnivPi := by
  ext f
  simp only [Finset.mem_pi, Finset.mem_image]
  exact ⟨λ hf ↦ ⟨λ i ↦ f i (Finset.mem_univ i),
    Fintype.mem_piFinset.mpr λ i ↦ hf i (Finset.mem_univ i), rfl⟩,
    λ ⟨g, hg, hgf⟩ i _ ↦ hgf ▸ Fintype.mem_piFinset.mp hg i⟩

omit [DecidableEq R] in
theorem piFinset_zero (s : Fin 0 → Finset R) : Fintype.piFinset s = {(![] : Fin 0 → R)} := by
  ext f
  simp only [Fintype.mem_piFinset, Finset.mem_singleton]
  exact ⟨λ _ ↦ Subsingleton.elim f _, λ _ i ↦ Fin.elim0 i⟩

theorem piFinset_succ (n : Nat) (s : Fin (n + 1) → Finset R) :
    Fintype.piFinset s =
      (s 0).biUnion (λ a ↦ (Fintype.piFinset (s ·.succ)).image (Fin.cons a)) := by
  ext f
  simp only [Fintype.mem_piFinset, Finset.mem_biUnion, Finset.mem_image]
  exact ⟨λ hf ↦ ⟨f 0, hf 0, (f ·.succ), (hf ·.succ), funext (Fin.cases (by simp) (by simp) ·)⟩,
    λ ⟨_, _, _, _, hgf⟩ ↦ hgf ▸ Fin.cases (by simpa) (by simpa)⟩

example (a b : R) :
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 3)).pi (λ _ ↦ ({a, b} : Finset R)) =
      {toUnivPi ![a, a, a], toUnivPi ![a, a, b], toUnivPi ![a, b, a], toUnivPi ![a, b, b],
       toUnivPi ![b, a, a], toUnivPi ![b, a, b], toUnivPi ![b, b, a], toUnivPi ![b, b, b]} := by
  simp only [univ_pi_eq_image_piFinset, piFinset_succ, piFinset_zero,
    Finset.biUnion_insert, Finset.singleton_biUnion,
    Finset.image_insert, Finset.image_singleton, Finset.singleton_union, Finset.insert_union,
    Matrix.Fin.cons_vecCons, Matrix.Fin.cons_vecEmpty]

example (a b c : R) :
    (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 3)).pi ![{a, b}, {b, c}, {c}] =
      {toUnivPi ![a, b, c], toUnivPi ![a, c, c], toUnivPi ![b, b, c], toUnivPi ![b, c, c]} := by
  simp only [univ_pi_eq_image_piFinset, piFinset_succ, piFinset_zero,
    Matrix.cons_val_zero, Matrix.cons_val_succ,
    Finset.biUnion_insert, Finset.singleton_biUnion,
    Finset.image_insert, Finset.image_singleton, Finset.singleton_union, Finset.insert_union,
    Matrix.Fin.cons_vecCons, Matrix.Fin.cons_vecEmpty]

Okay my reading is simproc is “like” writing your own tactic, but simp can invoke it, simp helps with the recursive traversal (apply the proc at every level), and some syntactic sugar makes it look less scary…?

That said, the method above is rather limited: suppose I want to prove a theorem of the form

example (a b c d : R) : ({a, b, c, d} : Finset R) = {c, b, a, a, d} := by sorry

I suppose I would need to write a tactic.

But writing a tactic seems to be harder in general. (I was reading through the compute_degree tactic and it looks really scary, even though it doesn't _sound_ that difficult on paper. I suppose one reason is that it tries to be very general? Still, if one isn't that ambitious, it shouldn't be that difficult?)

For this you can use the following simp call:

import Mathlib

variable {R : Type*} [DecidableEq R]

theorem test (a b c d : R) : ({a, b, c, d} : Finset R) = {d, c, b, a, a} := by
  simp [Finset.insert_comm, ← Finset.insert_empty, -insert_empty_eq]

it essentially uses a variant of insertion sort (so O(n^2))

To be precise, it's this algorithm:

def simpSort (l : List α) (lt : α → α → Bool) : Option (List α) := do
  match l with
  | [] => l
  | a :: t =>
    let t ← simpSort t lt
    match t with
    | [] => some (a :: t)
    | b :: t' => if lt b a then simpSort (b :: a :: t') lt else some (a :: t)
partial_fixpoint

there's also a dedicated tactic ac_rfl for these kinds of goals:

import Mathlib

variable {R : Type*} [DecidableEq R]

theorem test (a b c d : R) : ({a, b, c, d} : Finset R) = {d, c, b, a, a} := by
  simp only [← Finset.singleton_union]
  ac_rfl
... which uses another variant of insertion sort
but I suppose it's a bit faster since it uses kernel reduction
